props.title: The First Great Train Robbery

sections.content: The First Great Train Robbery marks a brilliant entry in the Victorian heist genre, with Sean Connery masterfully portraying Edward Pierce, the gentleman thief who orchestrated history's first moving train robbery. Michael Crichton adapts his own novel and directs with clockwork precision, creating a sophisticated caper that influenced later period heist films like The Prestige (2006) and Sherlock Holmes (2009). The film's meticulous attention to 1850s London's class dynamics and industrial revolution technology sets it apart from conventional heist movies.

movies.slug: The groundbreaking 12-minute silent film that pioneered narrative cinema

sections.content: The Victorian era proved fertile ground for sophisticated crime narratives, with The First Great Train Robbery paving the way for films like From Hell (2001) and The Illusionist (2006). These movies share a fascination with class mobility and emerging technologies of the industrial age. Connery's Pierce represents the criminal as gentleman scientist, using his understanding of the era's mechanical innovations to orchestrate an ingenious theft.

The film's influence extends beyond period pieces into modern heist classics. Heat (1995) echoes its methodical planning sequences, while Inside Man (2006) mirrors its interest in the social implications of crime. Crichton's direction emphasizes authenticity in both technical details and historical atmosphere, creating a template for intelligent crime films that balance entertainment with historical accuracy. sections.content: Following The First Great Train Robbery, Victorian-era crime films experienced a renaissance. Gangs of New York (2002) explored similar themes of class warfare and industrialization, while Sweeney Todd (2007) embraced the darker aspects of Victorian London. These films share a common thread in depicting how technological progress and social upheaval created new opportunities for ambitious criminals.
